utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Thank you all for co-operating in order for us to start very early in the morning. Let's start. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic, and please be as brief as possible and stop making comment, and please remember, you don't have to put every document in such a lengthy detail to the witness. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before I forget, I want to ask you something. Do we have your promise that you're going to look at your notes and diaries carefully and within a reasonable space of time be at the disposal of my Defence for contacts with it so that we can see what we can use from that material.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal possessions are currently held in storage, as my family and I moved from the Netherlands to another country. Therefore, I am not immediately able to get a hold of that material. Secondly, while I have kept most of my notebooks, I've never kept a diary but I've kept most of my notebooks, I don't know if all of them are there or some were lost. Certainly some were lost during the war, but at the earliest when we get our possessions I will certainly look through the notebooks. And if I believe that there is anything of consequence to my testimony that I've given over the last two days of this court, I would make it available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The very fact that you will be in contact with my Defence team means, I'm sure, that you'll be able to agree on what is important. Now, we have two more maps, map number 4 first that I'd like us to look at, and then map 6 from the Sarajevo-Karadzic binder. It's from the binder titled "Karadzic-Sarajevo map." One is a panorama, and the other is a detailed view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, can we have an additional one in case for the purpose of showing it to the witness in the future?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have the map books here. Mr. Reid has them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0424-9164 is the number. I assume it's the ERN number. But it's map number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that is 65 ter number 14665.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May we have it called up on e-court, please. I'm sorry, it's not actually a map. It's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we have it on our monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're in the same language, both of them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, could you briefly -- or, rather, could you mark the military hospital where you were. Do you see it there? That's right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you point out the Unis high-rises.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the government building, please, the Executive Council, as we called it, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mark that in for us, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the parliament building, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Holiday Inn Hotel next, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Hum hill next, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the hill you mentioned yesterday with the relay station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, with the well-known relay station.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know where Velesici is? It's the eastern slope from Hum, the densely populated little area there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you asked me beforehand, I would not, but now that you've pointed out what it is, then it must be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, underneath this -- these long-distance transmission lines, you have a hill there to the right.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you put a number 8 there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the name of the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the name of the hill, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Grdonj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate it before marking it to see if you know what I mean, what I'm referring to, by the long-distance transmission lines.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you referred to yesterday and when I said that on that map I was not able.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have it with the cursor first, please. And can you see the hill on this photograph, and is it Grdonj?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I didn't know. If you tell me it's Grdonj, I'm willing to believe it, but I don't actually know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Never mind then. Thank you. Now, do you agree that number 1 is the military hospital that you were in for a time, number 2 are the two Unis towers, number 3 is the government building of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 4 is the parliament building of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 5 is the Holiday Inn hotel, 6 is Hum hill, 7 is Velesici; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've just marked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we have photograph number 6 which shows this in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before pulling up another --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Date, signature, and I'd like to tender it first, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I tender it into evidence and have this recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit D213.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may this be given a number, please. And then may we have map 6 from this same binder called up on e-court. Well, not a map, a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think just to be clear we're talking about 0617-1145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. That is 65 ter number 21215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe we'll get through this quickly as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a part of Sarajevo that you know well. Yes. Thank you. That's it. Now, could you mark in the Unis towers on this photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to number it? Would you like me to number it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps number 1, please, to move from right to left.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the government building or Executive Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The parliament or Assembly. So government building is number 2. The Assembly number 3.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you see the bridge at Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that in as well, please. The entrance to the street running towards the church?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you see a part of the Catholic church at Marin Dvor which is to the very right edge of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mark that in, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's the route you take to go to the military hospital; right? Upwards and to the right; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did make a turn and then at a certain moment there's another turn to the left that we made, but that's further along and off this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Thank you. Could you now mark in the faculty of philosophy opposite the government building. Do you remember that that's what it was, the faculty of philosophy?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never taken into the faculty of philosophy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now mark in the Holiday Inn, please.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 6. And the technical school, please. Could you mark that in.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I was never taken to the technical school. It was along the front lines, but I was never taken there. And this is not an area of town, Your Honours, I ever walked through. We drove through it at high speed only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know where it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, it's in the region to the left of the Holiday Inn which I've marked with number 6. I believe that slightly down to the left is the museum, was the museum, but the precise location of the technical school I don't know, and I wasn't ever taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it's that large building with the courtyard to the left? You were quite right there. It's to the left and opposite the hotel.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just said, I was never taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you mark in both museum buildings.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, and again I have not been taken there, these were the museum buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Seven is the museum compound. Now could you mark in where the Marsal Tito Barracks were. It's not there any longer. They're obviously doing some construction work there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Marsal Tito Barracks is number 8. Now, behind the Marsal Tito Barracks do you see the railway station?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another place I never visited, but certainly there was the railway yard behind the Marsal Tito Barracks, and I imagine that you're - shall I mark it as 9 ? - you are referring to that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That's a well-known building in the city. Now, can you mark in next the so-called Sniper Alley, and mark that as number 10, Sniper Alley. Or perhaps you could draw a circle around Sniper Alley and indicate its borders and the scene where the most important events involving the snipers was.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of one scene that is the most important events involving the snipers. There was sniping all along the Marsal Tito Bulevar which runs there. It's that road. But I'm not aware of one scene, as you put it, but that's the road. Do you want me to put a 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Number 10. Now, do we agree that it's between the museum building and the Holiday Inn, that that was the main part where the shooting took place? And if that is so, could you draw a circle round that whole area between the museum and the Holiday Inn, which was considered the most dangerous place in town.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can mark that in a with number 11.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like ask you this, Mr. van Lynden: This --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we finished with the pen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I do believe we are, yes. I can just tell you that the technical school is that older building, and the faculty of philosophy, but it's not essential for us to mark them in. But perhaps you could put the date there and your signature, and let's stay with the photograph on the screen, because I have one more question to ask in that regard.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. van Lynden, from where is it that the Serbs could have shot at this particular place?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From roughly where the photograph was taken, the higher buildings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean that corner building below number 11 but on the Serb side. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- in the photograph, the river Miljacka is visible. As far as I'm aware, along that line, that was the front line. There are high buildings there, but the territory -- the ground rises up, and there were clear views down into the square. Indeed, in one of the stories that I filed while with your forces in September 1992, we -- the cameraman took shots and you see the streets directly below.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's right. Now, could you indicate the Miljacka River bed which was the front line. On one side you had the Serbs and on the other the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point of the city, yes. It is -- I mean, I marked Vrbanja village which is across the river Miljacka. So would you like me to make another marking? I mean, I can do here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. For the participants to see where the Miljacka River bed was. Yes, number 12. That's right. Now, in the Holiday Inn, is that where most of the foreign journalists were put up?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- as far as I'm aware, it's where most of the foreign journalists stayed. I'm not aware of any of them being put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. van Lynden. Now, this part of the street which was referred to as Sniper Alley, did it inflict great political damage on us in view of everything that went on there? Did it do us a lot of harm?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not for me to decide. That's a political question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, do you think that we were stupid enough to keep shooting ourselves in the foot and cutting our nose to spite our face? Now -- well, in doing something that was causing us harm -- or, rather, that called a world sensation. Now, to do this right in front of the very noses of all those journalists on that particular part of the street.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not going to comment on that. I know that there was shooting -- there were periods that there wasn't shooting, for instance, in 1994 in Sarajevo, and I actually once walked across Marin Dvor Square towards the end of March 1994. That's the only walk I ever did there during the war, but I know that there was shooting at all other times of the war. I'm not going to comment whether I think you were stupid and shooting yourselves in the foot. That is up for others, and is yourselves, to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now do you confirm or deny that along the very edge of the church there was a legitimate target, and the Unis towers, Executive Council building, parliament building, that there was a sniper and mortar on the museum building, the technical school and in the Marsal Tito Barracks and at the corner of the street leading from Dobrinja towards the church? Do you exclude this possibility, or do you allow for the possibility that there was significant military installations and that there was shooting against us from those areas?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware, and I think I have testified to that account yesterday, that after the evacuation of the Marsal Tito Barracks, I on one occasion in July 1992 saw machine-gun fire, rifle fire coming from the Marsal Tito Barracks in response to a shooting incident further down the main Bulevar. That would be to the left of the photograph that is now in front of us. So that would point that there were soldiers of the Bosnian Army in that building. I did not see when I was in the Unis towers - I went in there before the evacuation of the Marsal Tito Barracks - any troops. I'm aware that these are front line positions on the Bosnian side and that there is a great likelihood that they did, indeed, have military installations in them of one sort or another, whether it be snipers or mortars. I didn't personally see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. van Lynden --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd like to tender this into evidence first, please, Your Excellencies. I hope the participants now have a clearer picture of this part town that is mentioned all the time in the indictment and in many other documents. But can I tender this first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. There will be admitted as Exhibit D1214.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, are we finished with this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have finished with the photograph. Now, can I ask you this. Did you have a look at the articles in the course of last night that I gave you and, and if so, may we have them back?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have them with me. You may have them back, and, yes, I did look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. van Lynden, that you understand that I can't but go on to explain some of the things that you said or ask you about some of the things that you said during the examination-in-chief, and I hope to get through that fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, objection, Your Honours. We weren't told, and no reason why we should have been, which documents were given to Mr. van Lynden last night. I just ask, I don't know if Mr. Karadzic doesn't go through them all, could we, at the end, some point have on the record which exhibits were given to the witness to review before the continuation of his cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll bear that in mind during the course of cross-examine. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's of any use, perhaps Mr. Nicholls could take a look at these documents. They have their numbers. They're on e-court. But while I'm dealing with the transcript, perhaps he could take a look at them, and I can dictate the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Hand them over to the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you that on page 16, line 15 of the transcript of the direct examination -- oh, yes. We've finished that. Sorry. Let's have a look at page 18 now. I'm a bit perplexed by one of your assertions on the first day, the examination-in-chief. That was the 19th, wasn't it. Page 18. I'm a bit perplexed by your argument that at a particular location there weren't any snipers. I'd like to read that out now: "[In English] I had already, from my experience in 1991 in the former Yugoslavia, noticed that Yugoslav soldiers or whatever their nationality or religious background were, usually do not very careful in tidying up after themself, and therefore it seems likely to us that if there had been snipers in the building, we would find empty cartridge cases. That was not the case." [Interpretation] Is that sufficient to conclude that there were no snipers at a particular location?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot conclude definitively that there were no snipers at those locations. I was referring, if I remember correctly, to the military hospital, and that we checked whether it had been used as a military -- by the military at any time before we entered it. I can check as well as I can. I can ask as many people, and I come to a certain conclusion whether that building is safe for me -- or relatively safe for me and the crew to work in, and we reached that conclusion. During the entire time that we stayed in that hospital, I never saw military in that hospital unless they were brought there when they were wounded. And to the best of my knowledge, it was not used, at least when I was in that building, as a base for sniping or any kind of fire from government-held Sarajevo towards the lines held by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, the distinguished Mr. Nicholls asked you: "[In English] And while you were there staying there from the end of May, early June onwards, was the hospital targeted and hit by fire?" [Interpretation] May I ask you whether that means that before the hospital was taken over by the Muslim side there was no firing at the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the hospital being taken over by the Muslim side. Throughout my time in -- in Sarajevo, within the hospital, Muslims, Catholics, and Orthodox worked in that hospital. Indeed, when I first entered it the two chief surgeons, one of them was Muslim and the other was Orthodox, or Serb, if you like. So I'm not aware of it being taken over, as you put it, by the Muslims. I don't think -- believe that every happened. It was run by the same people who had worked there before. A number of those who had worked there before left, true, but I'm not aware of it having been taken over. Before I arrived, it's -- the building had clearly been hit on numerous occasions. The first time we went there we filmed the building, and that showed that it had sustained considerable damage. We filmed inside the building and filmed the office of one former doctor there who had been in the Yugoslav Army. His uniform was still hanging there. And that office had been hit by a large projectile because it had basically been completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Dr. Nakas took the hospital over on the 10th of May and that the entire security of the military hospital that had belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army got killed on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, which Dr. Nakas are you referring to? There are two of them, brothers. When I arrived there, Abdulah Nakas was the chief surgeon, and Bakir Nakas was serving as the director of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bakir Nakas was the director of the hospital from the 10th of May onwards when the Yugoslav People's Army had left the hospital. Up until then, it was the property of the Yugoslav People's Army, and it was guarded by a small JNA unit. That unit got killed. All of its members got killed on the 2nd of May? Did you know about that? And the commander, Lazarevic, when he was wounded, he committed suicide.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there at the beginning of May, so I cannot comment on something that I did not bear witness to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I believe that you did ask about what had happened three weeks before you came at such an important location. All right. So you didn't know about that; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware, was told, that there had been a withdrawal of a number of people from the hospital. Others had decided to stay. The precise events I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But on page 26, at one point you say: "[In English] We were told that first one person had been shot and wounded and the second person --" [Interpretation] And so on. So you are talking about things that you hadn't seen, but that you had been told about. Believe me, the fate of the military hospital and its security detail is so striking that I simply cannot understand how come they hadn't informed you about that. So it's not that you had to be a witness, but simply in the course of your duties as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this. You say we were told that first one person had been shot and wounded and the -- and so on. I'm not sure what you're referring to here. Can you first clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that you did not always talk about things that you had seen yourself only, but you also talked about things that you had heard about.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in order for the witness to answer your question correctly, you should remind him what he said on the first day. I take it it's page 2399 on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 26 on the first day, line 5. It has to do with that group that had been hit by sniper fire. You accepted information about that, about what had happened before you could have seen it yourself. "We were told." That is what I found striking. You said, "We were told." So you were told certain things. Did you hear anything about the military hospital? Were you told about the military hospital? Did you know that the military hospital was in JNA hands for a month, from the 6th of April onwards, and that it was fired at, at the time when it was in JNA hands?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly in reference to the "We were told," Your Honours, what I said then, this was a scene that I actually saw. I saw three people who had been hit by snipers who were still alive, lying on the ground. We were told, I said, that one person came out, a second person went to help the first person after they'd been shot, a third person went out. I think that was something that we then witnessed what happened and that finally those people were shot dead, and we followed them to hospital. That was an incident that, although I didn't see all of it, we were there for a part of it, also when those people actually died. As far as the hospital is concerned, no, I'm not aware that there was this incident that you're referring to in May. I was not given that detail while we were there. We did ask. The precise details we were not given, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But since they had not informed you, you were supposed to infer that it was the Serbs who had fired at the military hospital and left it pockmarked; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The damage that we saw when we first went to the military hospital on the outside was not equivalent to a gun battle at close range with rifles or machine-guns. This was far heavier weaponry that had hit the building and all the various floors, specifically the middle of the building or the middle to upper part of the building. And that was not -- much heavier weaponry was involved in that. There may, as you say, have been a gunfight that occurred there. But my experience of gun fights in cities would leave quite different markings on those buildings than the ones that we saw. There were also bullet holes, but most of it was heavier damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You rule out the possibility of the Green Berets using rifle grenades, hand grenades, mortars, and even heavy guns; right? You believe that they could not have had, say, a recoilless gun that can easily be placed in an apartment, for instance.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not rule that out, but the damage that would be caused to a building by the use of rifle grenades, hand grenades, is quite different to that on a building with rockets or artillery grenades. It -- there's a significant difference. There may have -- I'm not discounting, Mr. Karadzic, that there may have been a gun battle, as you say, before I arrived there, but it would have been carried out -- even if they were using, for instance, RPG 7 rockets, the damage to the building would have been of a different nature than what I now saw. Some of the damage that I saw would indeed bear you out in that. There was small arms and rocket, anti-tank rocket, damage, but there was -- most of the damage was of a much heavier nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In my previous question in the transcript it says "hand grenades." I thought I had actually said hand-held launchers, or, rather, Zoljas and Osas, but anyway. On page 27, toward the bottom, you mention a very touching story about a Muslim girl and a Serb man who got killed when they were crossing over to Grbavica. Did you see that yourself, or were you told about this?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to that in answer to the question by the Prosecution as to the newsworthiness of sniping events. That incident happened when I was not in Sarajevo. I did not personally report on that incident. I was made aware of it from -- by general press reports. I was just -- my reference to it was simply saying that unless there were specific reasons, many of the sniping events were no longer considered newsworthy. I was just differentiating in answer to the Prosecution, but I did not witness that particular incident myself, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but that really was something that we all knew about because it was such a touching thing. Do we agree that the Muslim man -- Muslim woman and Serb man were trying to cross over to flee to Grbavica, the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you, Mr. Karadzic, I wasn't there and I did not report on this particular incident. You may well be right, but right now I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. Who could be accused of having killed them, the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I can't -- I wasn't there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But if that's the way it was, it would seem that the Serbs had killed the two lovers, the Serb man and the Muslim woman, who wanted to cross over to their side, and that never happened, that somebody would kill someone who was fleeing towards them. I'm right, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is that your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the only question is whether we can leave things so unclear that suggest that it is the Serbs that are to be blamed. Can you be more specific? If we say something, we have to be very specific in order to dispel. Are there any doubts there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness said he doesn't know. Move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 28, towards the end, from line 20 onwards, Mr. Nicholls asked you to clarify -- this is what he said: "[In English] I may have misspoke, Your Honour. That is correct that -- thank you. I just --" [Interpretation] Then: "[In English] Just hours after the evacuation of the troops from the Marshall Tito barracks --" [Interpretation] And further on it says: "[In English] Among the cities ancient minarets the rockets fell heralding another night of heavy shelling. [Interpretation] Do you agree that the Marsal Tito Barracks was full of military weaponry, equipment, APCs, plus 600 rifles that a JNA general had brought in, in order to get the cadets out? Do you believe that the barracks was empty from the moment of the evacuation, or do you think that it was taken over by the Green Berets straight away? So what is it that you opt for? Was it empty?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I was not taken into the Marsal Tito Barracks after its evacuation, and therefore I cannot state what was or what was not left inside it. What we saw was that fairly shortly after the evacuation had been completed was that it became a target for -- of a heavy artillery barrage. We filmed people running out of it. Therefore, it is -- it seems pretty likely to us, and I would agree with you therefore, that certain elements of the Bosnian Army had gone in immediately after its evacuation. We were not there ourselves to see who these people were. We filmed this from the military hospital, but we clearly showed people running out of the barracks, and we showed the barracks then becoming the main target of the shelling that night. The shelling that night, also shells fell in other districts that had absolutely nothing to do with the Marsal Tito Barracks or the evacuation of the troops from those barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that video-clip it says page 29, lines 11 and 12: "[In English] This is the scene of wholesale devastation of a city being obliterated while the world watched -- watches but does nothing." [Interpretation] Is this some kind of a reprimand to the world? Is it a call for intervention?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was basically a statement of fact. The city was being shelled, and as far as I could see, the outside world was not doing anything to halt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say that the world was doing nothing, do you mean that they were supposed to intervene militarily?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant that they had to intervene in one manner or another to see to it that the shooting stopped, which would seem to me in the interest of all parties concerned. That could be done in various ways, and that is -- I'm not a government or the United Nations. What we saw at that time was a situation in Sarajevo where the city was being shelled, and it seemed to us that the world had turned its back -- that the world's governments had turned their back on the city and what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you film that first clip, that heavy shelling during the night? I think it was 65 ter 4264C. The part that we're talking about, that is. Did you film that, or did you get that footage from someone else?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what 65 ter -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is the film to which you commented this is the scene of wholesale devastation of a city being obliterated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. All the pictures and all those stories that were shown on Wednesday afternoon to this Court were filmed by the Scaranese [phoen] cameraman, except for when it came to the story of the 5th of December, 1992. In that case, pictures from other camera crews, and I already testified that it was, for instance, the shelf an apartment block being hit, that the wider shot was taken by a CNN cameraman, but there were other pictures in that story that were taken by other camera crews. But all the stories from June 1992 were filmed solely by us. I believe at that time we were the only foreign television crew inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what happened on the 5th of June was something that you had filmed directly. So practically you were filmed at the same time, you yourself and the shells falling behind you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't recall whether there were shells falling behind me when I did the piece to camera, stand-up, as it is called in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see that first clip of the 5th of June. I think that 4264C is the 65 ter number. While we're waiting for that, let me ask you, Mr. van Lynden, you filmed that from the military hospital. That is to say that you are facing that area. Is it correct that all the shells on that footage are falling from your right-hand side to your left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll play that now if that's what Mr. Karadzic would like. That's P929, if I kept my numbers straight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "These ancient minarets, the rockets fall heralding an another night of heavy shelling."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you stop here just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these shots horizontal and at the level of your own eyes, or of your camera, rather?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I wasn't the cameraman. These shots were taken from what, if I'm looking towards Grbavica, would be the right hand balcony of the building. As far as I'm aware the cameraman would see to it -- and it was filmed on a tripod at all times, as much as possible to keep the camera as steady as possible, not off the shoulder. And, therefore, he would obviously try to get the camera straight. That said, he was in an exposed position, and sometimes the camera could maybe not be completely straight. It's not the same as in a peacetime situation being able to look at everything and see to it that the tripod is completely straight, but basically, yes, it is. So on the right-hand side and the shots were jumping from left to right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these shells falling into town, or are they going horizontally from the eastern part of town towards the western part of town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're coming from the southern part of town, the southern hills, into the city, away from -- towards the more -- well, the centre and the western part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're in the in the centre, and --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So to the west of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go on. Sorry, while -- just a moment, please. What -- is this -- what shell is this?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is heavy machine-gun, possibly light anti-aircraft fire, but precisely I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just before we move on, can I, for the record, say we were at 07:54:2 is the frame we were discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we do agree that this is going from the lower parts of the southern hills, as you said. It's not going from town. Actually, it's ascending, as it were.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is from the lower hills on the southern side and is, to a degree, ascending, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "For the next six hours there is no let-up."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where these explosions took place, are they Vraca looking at it from your vantage point, half to the right above Grbavica; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well -- no. No, no, no, no, no, no. No, no. These are all on the other side of the river Miljacka, Mr. Karadzic. No, this is all incoming into the part of Sarajevo held by the Bosnian government. All the areas to the west of us, not to the south of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May we go back 30 seconds. Let's see it again so that we can establish where the explosions took place, and you'll see from the reports that all the houses in Vraca were destroyed that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If that's fine with Mr. Karadzic, we'll start there, which is at 07:51:01.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "For the next six hours there is no let-up."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. Where those explosions are. Half to the right, south-west of where you were. Is that where the Serb settlement of Vraca was or is?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the shot immediately preceding this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we go back a few seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is edited pictures, edited without my presence. Without me seeing the entire film, I can not precisely say what that one -- whether one shot was. We moved from one balcony to the other depending on the level of fire in one district or another. I can't answer that question. The earlier ones were the longer sequence, but this was one shot. You may be right, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this is the first time that I hear that this was edited, that it's not an authentic --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All television stories are edited, Mr. Karadzic. We filmed for hours that night. The piece was 2 minutes and something. All television news reports are edited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to locate the time-frame where we saw that blast? It's around 8 minutes, 20 to 25. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we see the footage to the end, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What's this? What's this, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a light grenade. Grenades fired, probably from a mortar. That gives illumination. Illumination grenade. There are different names given to it. They can be fired from 60-, 81-, 82-millimetre, possibly from 120, I don't have experience with 120-millimetre mortars. They usually last for several minutes. It hangs on a small parachute and gives light depending on -- on the calibre of the mortar it's fired from, equivalent to hundreds of thousands of candles, and it burns usually for a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you think that that was one of ours, one of our light grenades?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How am I meant to know? As far as I'm aware, you, the Bosnian Serb Army, had a great deal more heavy weaponry and a great deal more ammunition, but I am not discounting the possibility that this light grenade, this particular light grenade, was fired by the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's play some more to the end, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I just put it on, sorry. It's 08:27:04 is the still image that we've been discussing. And if Mr. Karadzic could say stop in English when he wants us to stop, that would be quicker for Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very helpful. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "The city is hit from every side by practically every imaginable projectile."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is this horizontal fire, the lower line, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again either heavy machine-gun fire or fire from light anti-aircraft guns that were usually truck-mounted and used, and I saw them repeatedly when I was with your forces as used horizontally, not against the aircraft because the Bosnian didn't have any aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, I note that we stopped at 8 minutes, 42 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how come these illuminated circles are so large for such small calibres?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking heavy machine-guns or we're talking about 20-, 30-, or 40-millimetre. That's not such a small calibre. It's not a rifle bullet. It is considerably bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have to play any more of this. Just let me ask you, Mr. van Lynden, what position could we have held so low to the left of the military hospital in Sarajevo, that low down? Did you know where our positions were, and from what position did this firing come from? To the left, east of the military hospital at the level of the military hospital, that low?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is -- these shots are coming in to the part of town west of the military hospital, and they emanated, as I already said, from the southern part of Sarajevo, the hills specifically. This wasn't from a low point. This was from a relatively high point. It didn't come from the banks of the river Miljacka. These came from higher positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But they're coming in from the east, never mind the slope, east of the military hospital, east of the military hospital. The direction is east/west, right? It's not going north/south. If it went north/south, it would be over your heads.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was going south/north, it would be going over our heads. This was coming from the south, sometimes directly south of where we were, sometimes slightly more to the east, south-east of where we were from that -- the hillside into town. And on these particular pictures, to the west of us, but we had other images of rockets landing to the east of us in the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in where the projectiles are going horizontally from south-east to north-west, but flying horizontally at the level of the military hospital. Do we agree there that this is horizontal fire?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just about, yes, but I mean, it -- it -- this is fire emanating to the south of where we are and then striking targets to the west of where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they're hitting south too. They're moving horizontally from east to west on this screen; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that it's not as if they're going straight in front us in the hospital, no. They're coming from south of the hospital, possibly somewhat south-east, but not from the east straight by us, no. They're coming from the south into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is the direction of this fire, not in relation to the military hospital but to the azimuth. Is it south/north or east/south-west -- north-west?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say south to north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But then the fire would have gone over your heads and not --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- flying past you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the fire did fly past us, and the buildings we were in were also repeatedly hit. So there was fire straight from south to north. But on this occasion, this was fire at some distance away from us as the images clearly show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, we don't need that clip any more. I think we've seen enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 30, you say: "[In English] You could see it coming down on the city." [Interpretation] On the city. And then to the end of the page you say something specific and say that you couldn't see such things anywhere else, and: "[In English] We had never been able to capture such footage of fighting or of artillery. It should give an indication that this was really an extremely heavy night of shelling as were the nights that followed." [Interpretation] But you stand by what you said, that what came from the hill and was falling on the city was Serb fire; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, just a small error in the translation. Never been able to "capture" such footage, not "counter" such footage on page 2404.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In answer to your question, firstly I related this footage to my own personal past and what I had experienced in other war zones, and throughout my career as a war correspondent, I have never been able, as a television correspondent, to be able to capture such amounts of artillery, machine-gun fire coming down on a city. As I tried to explain on Wednesday, filming in war zones is not the same as making a Hollywood movie. It is a complex business. We don't decide where the shells are going to land. We have to react to them. And to be able to get so much on camera showed that this was extremely heavy shelling. The -- when I spoke of "you saw it coming," I'm referring specifically to the rocket fire coming from the top of the mountains to the east of Sarajevo onto the city, and we showed those rockets not only being fired but where they landed. Again, that's fairly unusual in my personal experience. I do not discount that some of the fire would also have been directed towards Serb areas, but I didn't see a barrage of heavy weaponry directed at the southern hills of Sarajevo that were controlled by your forces. I saw an intense barrage coming down on top of Sarajevo, the Sarajevo that was controlled by the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said on page 32 that -- that the mortar was overshooting, then undershooting, and then hitting the target? So do you mean to say that at first go, first try, they can't hit the target, first time round?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring then to -- that was not mortar fire, that was artillery fire that hit the railway yard. Of course an artillery unit can hit something first time round. On the whole, my experience is that it takes a few shells for a particular artillery piece to hit its precise target. It is why there are artillery observers or spotters who will tell the crew to change the level of their gun. My experience as a mortar commander is that the first one either lands short or long. You then try to bring it in or further out. Again, usually the second doesn't hit the target. And if you have an extremely good crew, then on the third time you do hit the precise target you are aiming for. What we saw on that day, this is just after the evacuation of the Marsal Tito Barracks, were the first artillery rounds that were long on the railway -- hitting the railway yard. They were clearly told to change the level of their guns, and afterwards they hit the target which they were aiming for, on that occasion the Marsal Tito Barracks, and from what we could see, they were extremely accurate after that with their fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, with that answer, we'll take our first break for today for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may very briefly. I don't want to slow anything down. I hope, I truly hope we're able -- for the witness's sake that we're able to finish completely today. If that is the case, if possible, I'd request no more than seven minutes of redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Trying to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, this is such a valuable witness that I'm not sure that I'll be able to get through in the time I have, but let's try. On page 35 of the 19th of May, you say: "[In English] Every night in Sarajevo you think it can't be worse, but it does, making a mockery of the attempts of mediators to bring peace to the city which is unfolded in war. Less than 24 hours earlier the Serb commanders had put their signatures on the agreement," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Therefore, what you're suggesting is that somebody is making a mockery of the attempts and efforts of the mediators, and I agree with that, but can you tell me who you had in mind when you said that? Who avoided peace conferences and a peaceful solution? The Serbs or the Muslims? It's a simple answer. Let's leave the Croats to one side for the moment. Just the Serbs or the Muslims, which?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't referring -- I said that the fighting and the escalating scale of the fighting as we saw it and witnessed it at that time seemed to us to make a mockery of the attempts of both the European Union and the United Nations to bring peace to a city that was clearly enfolded in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the next paragraph you say less than 24 hours earlier you suggest that the Serb commanders signed cease-fires and then failed to respect it and that their shooters kept firing. Now, do you know of the official position taken by the United Nations according to which 90 per cent of the cease-fire agreements were violated by the Muslim side and on the Serb side and that almost 100 per cent of offensives in the town of Sarajevo were launched by the Muslim side? And those are facts and figures from the United Nations, UNPROFOR. Were you aware of that, and does that suggest that it was the Serb commanders who violated the cease-fires they signed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were informed by the people we spoke to at the United Nations at that time that Serb commanders had signed a cease-fire and that, as far as the UN at that time could see, it had been broken by Serb fire. I'm not referring to the entire war. This was just really still at the beginning of the war, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But let me remind you of something. The Muslim documents from the beginning of June, from the 1st of June right up to the 20th of June, that we displayed several days ago clearly show that on the one hand they signed, and on the other hand they continued their actions just as if Hasan Efendic had signed nothing. Halilovic continued his offensive, and we have a lot of minutes and transcripts where they say Milinkladska is light. We've taken their barracks at Nedzarici almost completely. How then can we accept that these were Serb violations when they were in fact Muslim violations? And now if you look at the bottom of that page, Mr. Nicholls, the distinguished Mr. Nicholls was very satisfied and said I think the correct remuneration was pretty self-explanatory. Therefore he understood it completely, and I believe everybody else in the courtroom understood you to have accused the Serbs of violating those cease-fires. Did you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have just said, we were told by those at the United Nations headquarters in Sarajevo at that time that on those days that's what had occurred, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I have to note that when Mr. Nicholls said it was self-explanatory, he must have referred to the boy who was lying on the table.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, we know nothing about the boy either, but I think he was referring to the entire clip. That's what I thought at least. But if we can briefly look at 1D01155 next, please. I think we've already had at that displayed, have we? On e-court. 1D01155 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were in Hadzici at the time, and this is a report from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the Main Staff. I'd like us to look at the first paragraph. It says: "Despite the cease-fire agreed in the Sarajevo sector, the enemy fired 15 shells at Ilidza and Nedzarici from the Hrasnica sector, and this was from the sector where UNPROFOR vehicles were supposed to pass. No other significant enemy activities were observed." Do you agree that this report confirmed that 15 shells did indeed fall on Serb settlements?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing I would point out that this has nothing to do with my report in June 1992. These are two completely separate matters. Does this report confirm that 15 shells landed at Ilidza and Nedzarici? I don't know if that report is accurate or not. I have not seen it before, and I wasn't -- as you yourself said, I was outside Hadzici. I wasn't in Ilidza and Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this report into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour, following the guidelines as I understand them. The witness has made clear he can't really comment on it, was not able to see it. He's able to say, Well, this report says what it says, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. Same rule. We will not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D01154 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it refers to Hadzici, which is where you were. 1154 is the document number, 1D01154. Thank you. It says: "During the day the enemy fired artillery shots at a number of locations especially in Hadzici, Zenik, Vrelo Bosne, Vreoce, and Nedzarici sector. There was artillery fire and especially sniper fire, and Brownings were fired at Hadzici. In line with their orders, our forces did not return fire." Now, at that time you were in Hadzici, were you not? And did you see that Hadzici were being targeted? I think you reported on that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state whether I was in Hadzici on the 20th of September. I was in Hadzici during September with that precise date that I'm afraid, Mr. Karadzic, I don't remember. We were actually -- we didn't stay in the village, town, whatever Hadzici can be called, very long. We were sent to a unit of the Bosnian Serb forces in the hills, as I recall a forested area. I think I testified yesterday that when we came to that unit, no shooting was going on, and that that unit came under fire. We filmed that and we filmed their response, and they did return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add that when we were in Hadzici, it was not under shell-fire. We did not observe shell-fire when we were there. That does not exclude that it could have happened before or afterwards. We were not shown if it had happened earlier. We were simply taken to this one position in the hills in the forests, and there we filmed, as I have just testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this document admitted? Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness can't confirm the content of it. You will have another opportunity to introduce this document later. We will not admit this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now go on to page 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to draw your attention to page 37 of the 19th of May where you say in your video-clip: "Sarajevo is burning in its heart and its suburbs." [Interpretation] And lower down: "[In English] At the city's main hospital, the situation is even worse. The counter-offensive of the Bosnian Territorial Defence forces have run into a continual barrage," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] And then on page 38 you go on to say in response to Mr. Nicholls's question in the video-clip: "[In English] We saw at the beginning again more shelling, and you said words to the effect that the whole city becoming a target. Can you tell us if you remember which areas of the city?" [Interpretation] You say: "[In English] As I said, it was our impression that the whole city," and you repeat, and so on. First question: Do you still assert that this was a counter-offensive of the Muslim forces, or was it simply their offensive as such and a Serb counter-offensive, rather?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that they -- this is in the area where the maternity hospital had been. We couldn't actually go there, and we were not allowed to go there. We were told that they had launched a counter-offensive and that the men that we saw being brought in who had been wounded had come under a sustained barrage in response to that offensive. This was clearly a purely military affair taking place on the front lines. That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Answer to your first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Also, you said that that was your impression, that the entire city was a target. I asked you when we spoke before your testimony whether you saw Vukovar and whether you saw Mostar. How long did the war going on in Vukovar, and how long did it go on in Mostar? Two or three months in Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three, three and a half months in Vukovar, yes, which I did cover from the beginning until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Mostar?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not cover the battle for Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If Sarajevo as a whole would be a target, what would it look like after 1.300 days of war in your experience? What would Sarajevo look like after 1.300 days of war? On average reports said that at least 500 shells fell per day. So what would it have looked like in that case? Compared to Vukovar, for example, after three and a half months, or Mostar. And you saw the pictures of Mostar with empty buildings, totally destroyed buildings and so on.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're distorting my words. I said that on that particular night, it seemed to us that the entire city was the target because we saw shelling landing in -- right across the city. That was not the case on a daily basis for 1.300 days every war. It was the case on that particular night. How did Vukovar look after three and a half months of -- Vukovar was a small baroque town on the Danube, Your Honours, and it was very, very heavily shelled. I don't know the precise number of shells that fell on Vukovar, but most of Vukovar was reduced to rubble. As far as I have seen, large parts of Sarajevo were reduced to rubble, but Sarajevo, it was a different situation. It's a much bigger city than Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which part of Sarajevo was reduced to rubble? Can you give us at least one example?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Various parts were reduced to rubble. You had the "Oslobodjenje" building, the old library. Shells landed all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are saying that certain buildings were destroyed. However, my conclusion here was that you are saying that entire neighbourhoods were destroyed. As for individual buildings, we can agree on that. On page 37 you say Sarajevo is burning in its heart and in its suburbs. Do we agree that the Serbs held part of the heart and most of the suburbs of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that the Serbs held part of the heart and some of the suburbs of the city, but the areas that we saw burning were those within the area controlled by the Bosnian government. On that particular day. I'm not discounting that there were not fires in the territory held by you on other days, but on that particular day that is what we saw and filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 42 of the transcript of the 19th of May, you say that you were arrested at different check-points. Were you stopped, or were you arrested? And if you were arrested, why did you not inform your own station or me personally?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were arrested in the sense that we were not allowed to drive on, and we were told to go back to Pale. We did inform. You had, as I recall, even a minister for information. He was informed of this, that every time we went out, at a check-point we would be told that we could not go further and that we had to return to Pale. I meant arrested in that sense that we were not allowed to go to front lines to film, and we did absolutely inform the members of your administration who had to look after the foreign media. It's the reason that I spoke to you at the London Conference and then at the Intercontinental Hotel at the beginning of September in Belgrade to see to it that that kind of thing did not happen again, and that if we came, that we would be able to work and be able to film and interview Serbs, for them to put their case, Mr. Karadzic. And in September that, to a degree, worked, although again there were military units that we were not allowed to film at despite the fact that we were accompanied by two military policemen of your forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, no commander likes having civilians milling about his lines, especially not journalists, let alone foreign correspondents, but I would rather call that being stopped rather than being arrested. Would you not agree? It wasn't an arrest in the strict sense of the word, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the strict sense of the word, you're right. We were stopped and sent back. But we weren't put in gaol, for instance, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now draw your attention to page 44. You said that your colleagues from Serbian television attacked you not because of all your other reports but because in their opinion, it seems that you portrayed Juka Prazina as -- as some kind of a hero. What was his name now? Robinhood. Right. So they did not object to what you were doing, but to portray a rapist who threw people out of windows as well, well -- as a hero, well, they minded that. "[In English] Mr. Karadzic likely intervened in this conversation. The conversation also ranged about other matters, but it was for me an example of the strange mentality that seemed to have more people in their grip in Pale, that the story about a man who I described as one of the principal defenders of Sarajevo in that story done at the beginning of June, Juka Prazina who I mentioned was a convicted criminal, that they felt that this was a story that was against them." [Interpretation] And then -- yes. Would you agree that this is a characterisation of a group mentality, a national mentality, rather? I mean, it wouldn't be right if a psychiatrist said it, but nevertheless, you presented this characterisation of the Serb mentality in Pale; right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found it extremely strange that they were -- that the people that we spoke to in Pale and specifically at Pale television, were absolutely happy with the stores about Sarajevo being shelled, showing the wounded, et cetera, the stories that you are now arguing to me over these last two days, that there were inaccuracies in them. They never said there were inaccuracies in any of those stories. They were perfectly happy with those stories, while it would seem to us that those were stories that were not in the interests of the Bosnian Serb cause. The story of Juka Prazina, in which I make absolutely clear that he was a convicted criminal, was a story that would -- seemed to us and indeed seemed to people that I spoke to in London, Brussels, and The Hague, was a sorry in the interests of the Bosnian Serbs, and yet they inverted this. The stories that you have, in your defence, argued that I wasn't careful enough about were stories what they thought were fine. And the story that was in the interest of the Bosnian Serbs they thought was terrible and I was attacked about. We thought that was very strange, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I assume that you know of the work and reputation of David Binder of the "New York Times." Everybody else does as well. You have heard of Binder. You know Binder, do you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know Mr. Binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, he is very, very well known. He is a senior journalist. He wrote in the "New York Times" in June 1994: "It is politically right in New York and Washington to hit the Serbs whenever possible going up to a point when it becomes almost racist. Making Serbs notorious practically rules out the possibility of balanced reporting."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an old hand at journalism, a journalist from the "New York Times" that enjoys a very high reputation. What do you say to what he said?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not responsible for the statements Mr. Binder, whom I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But he is talking about correspondents who are reporting about the Serbs. He's not talking about the Serbs. I hope that doesn't pertain to you as well, although this characterisation of mentality reminded me of this, and that's why I actually quoted him, because this characterisation of a group mentality reminded me of this mildly racist approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Stop making comment, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do we have a 65 ter number for what he's reading from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is quotation from David Binder. It's a quotation from the "New York Times." If necessary, we'll show you the entire text, but I had not intended to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the point is not that. You have to inform the other parties of the documents you are going to use during your cross-examination as a principle. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just react to the comment that Mr. Karadzic made at the end there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't making a characterisation of a group mentality. I was describing what happened in relation the reaction of Bosnian Serbs to the stories that I filed at the beginning of June. They were anti one story, and they were perfectly happy with the rest. That's not a characterisation of a group mentality, Mr. Karadzic. And certainly not racism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 45, you say that I had said to you -- this is it: "[In English] He told me that the enclaves were unacceptable, that they had to become part of Serb territory." [Interpretation] Do you agree that on all maps the territory that you call enclaves was accepted by the Serbs to be in Muslim-held territory, the Cutileiro map, the Vance-Owen map, then Owen-Stoltenberg, that map was accepted. In all these maps, and primarily in Cutileiro's map, we accepted that that would be Muslim territory. As a matter of fact, I authorised President Milosevic to say that we did not care about Srebrenica, that in some version it could be within Muslim territory. Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked what you had said to me when we met, and I -- as I, to the best of my knowledge recall, you said that they were not acceptable. What you did elsewhere I was not asked about. I was asked what you had said to me, and as I recall those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to agree even more that your notes would be invaluable. Isn't that right? Now, let me draw your attention to page 50 --

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
