utterances.text: Are you asking a question? "Isn't that right," is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just supporting, corroborating my request to receive your notes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if I wrote notes about those meetings, Mr. Karadzic. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's on the record, and I'm challenging it. Now, let's look at page 52. Page 52. You are talking about the convent. On who's territory was it, with the nuns there that were giving coffee and food? On who's territory was that? Towards the end, you say: "[In English] The attacks by Serbs in this sector have diminished leaving the battalion commander exuding confidence." [Interpretation] On whose territory was this convent?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Serbs in -- I'm sorry, the line does not make any sense to me. By Serbs in this sector have diminished leaving the battalion --" as far as your question of the convent is concerned, it was in Bosnian Serb-held territory. The convent was in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Attacks -- [Interpretation] This is what you said, these are your words from the video-clip: "[In English] The string of little village lining the cemetery have been turned into bunkers, sitting room floors roughly redecorated with logs, although some are more imaginative. Some mirrors deployed for one guard to view all angles. Attacks by Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's correct. I will read out for you. "The string of little villas lining the cemetery have been turned into bunkers. Sitting room walls roughly redecorated with lines of logs, although some of the defences are more imaginative. Bathroom mirrors subtlety deployed to allow one guard to view all angles. All of late the tanks against the Serb lines in this sector have diminished, leaving the battalion commander exuding confidence." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, what it says here is "attacks by Serbs," not "on Serb lines," if we have the same transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcripts are corrected overnight, comparing the audio recording. So what I read out is the corrected version from the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I would just say, Your Honour, we do have the translation of that story, the transcript from that video, which accords with what Your Honour read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree then that this convent is on the Serb side, on Serb territory, and that those nuns were in territory where the Serbs had authority?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question as to the other part of the story that you've just -- that the Judge has just read out to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would not have had a question had the transcript been correct, because according to the version that I have, it had seemed that it was the Serbs who were attacking the area, whereas my assertion is that it was Serb-held territory attacked by the Muslims. We protected these nuns. We saved their library. We returned it at the end of the war, and we have proof of that throughout the war. Thank you. May I draw your attention to page 56. It's the transcript of the 19th. Mr. Nicholls asked you: "[In English] That you stated that it was a civilian target in the story we just watched. If you could just explain that. Did you see any indications there, any fire coming from that building or how you came to that conclusion?" [Interpretation] Answer: "[In English] Well, we were certainly by that stage of the war very much aware that whenever there was an incident in Sarajevo, the defence from the Bosnian Serb side would be that it had been a legitimate military target or that the Bosnians had been shooting at themselves. And this in December 1992 we are talking about, and so we were quite quick. I mean, we did this anyway. Wherever we went was the building used by elements of the Bosnian Army, we did not only meet this one distraught -- distraught man who you say in these pictures who lost his flat. We met other people in the flat, and they all -- they all went, are you mad to let the military use the building, because we know what the repercussion would be." [Interpretation] My question: Do you think that citizens in buildings in Sarajevo could decide whether somebody was going to shoot from that building or from a particular apartment or from the roof? Do you think that it was for the citizens to say, or did they simply have to accept everything that the Green Berets would decide? Is this sufficient to conclude that something was not a military target?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to one particular building and to the questions we asked and the answers that we got from the people living in that one particular building. We also went to the UNPROFOR headquarters to ask them whether any of their forces had seen fire emanating from that building that was targeted with incendiary rounds, and they said they had not. It is not a comment made about every single block of flats in the whole of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In another video-clip you said that the defenders had turned apartments and offices into places from where there was shooting, and that explains what you said just now, and I'll accept it.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no. Wait a second. On the front lines, as also on your side of the front lines, apartments and office blocks were turned into military installations. This was not a front-line apartment building. This was a civilian apartment building that was targeted. Quite different to the other positions on the -- right on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the killing of the wife of General Sefer Halilovic and her brother? They were killed on the terrace of their apartment. An attempt was made to portray this as being due to a Serb shell. Since Sefer Halilovic was a military officer, he managed to refute that and prove that it was an explosion. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and yes, we were also told that this was not done by Bosnian Serb fire, but that this had something to do with an internal power struggle. I wasn't in Sarajevo at the time, so I did not actually report on this myself, but I am aware of the incident happening and that the fire had come from, let's say, within the Bosnians' forces themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask for D162. It is General Rose's book that we'll be quoting often here. D162, page 18. So this is General Rose's book. Page 18: "[In English] Initial Muslim tactics --" [Interpretation] I'll start reading it before we get it in e-court: "[In English] As we crossed the conflict line on the Bosnian side a detachment of 120-millimetre mortar opened fire close by the road to our left. Bosnian forces were shelling Serb positions on the hills above the city. I asked rather nervously what was happening, and Victor Andreev, the Russian UN civilian advisor in Sarajevo, who had come to meet me and who was to become my inseparable friend and colleague, told me there was nothing to worry about. There was no such thing in the eyes of the Bosnian government, he explained, as a purely military action. There was only political action. They always greeted new arrivals to Sarajevo in this way, and the Serbs always responded in kind with artillery fire on the city. Visitors were thus given a practical demonstration of the aggression being committed against the state of Bosnia." [Interpretation] We maintain -- or, rather, in our interview you said that the weakness thesis of ours, our weakest position, was precisely that we said that they shot often, that they shot at their own people, that they employed trickery, and so on. We claim the same as Mr. Rose claims, that the basic goal of the Muslim forces and policy was to provoke foreign intervention and to blacken the Serbs, besmirch the Serbs, either by talking about killing or opening fire, and so on. Did [as interpreted] you feel uncomfortable when you realised that the Muslim government had duped you, tricked you? "Would you." In the transcript it says "did you?" Would you, would you feel uncomfortable if you were to realise that? Would you fell uncomfortable if they duped you the way we claim that you were duped by them? And I hope you weren't by us intentionally.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear it, Mr. Karadzic. I was never welcomed to Sarajevo in the manner that Mr. Rose thinks he was welcomed to Sarajevo. I cannot believe that what we witnessed at the beginning of June was done for my entertainment. I have not myself witnessed the same as Mr. Rose, and you would have to ask Mr. Rose and Mr. Andreev about their version of events. What I said to you on Tuesday afternoon was that the repeated claims you made was that basically the Bosnians only shot at themselves, they were never shot at by you is not something that holds up in my experience. The Bosnian were fired at enough by your forces; they didn't need to shoot at themselves to cause international outrage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 69 and 70 displayed, please, of this same book. And while we're waiting for that come up, I'll start reading: "[In English] Many journalists in Sarajevo also supported the war option either because they believed that it was morally right to engage in some form of holy war against the Serbs or else because images of war sell better than those of peace." [Interpretation] That's towards the end of page 69, the bottom of page 69, and then goes on to page 70. Now, how do you see this, this assessment made by the reporter from Sarajevo, an experienced journalist, General Rose, saying that it was different?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, General Rose was a soldier and not a journalist. It's his view. I cannot comment on his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'm saying that he as a soldier understood that the reporting was different from what he saw the situation to be as a soldier, which means he did not agree with the reporting.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's his business. You should ask him about that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the United Nations were one of the sources of information. So you could be informed through the United Nations. You could ask them for information, could you not?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1992, General Rose was not in Sarajevo. He arrived in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much longer do you have for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, two or three hours, but I see what the situation's like. So I'd like to ask you to ask Mr. van Lynden to come back, because then we could allow him to select entries from his notebooks. And although he was in Bosnia at certain periods, he's a very valuable witness, and we can use his example and the example of what he said to throw light, shed some more light on the situation. On many things, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I was told from the Registry and through Victims and Witnesses Section that they have -- because they have some special arrangement with the Schiphol Airport, you may leave around 12.00, leave the Tribunal around 12.00. Is it -- is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't been told that. I just know that I have a flight that I absolutely need to take this afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am aware of the time, but I was told -- I was confirmed by the Registry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one has told me about special -- deals at Schiphol Airport, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, just very briefly, I'm sorry. I haven't heard about that special arrangement or time or anything like that either. I just want to put my position, I strenuously do not want Mr. van Lynden to be too rushed. I don't want there to be any chance of him missing this flight whatsoever, and I would say that the accused has had just shy of 8 hours of cross-examination time. Regardless about how some of that time was used, he has had ample time to cross-examine this witness based on the statement and direct, two days of court time in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think he has had that many hours, but around -- I haven't checked, but I -- it's better to save on -- to err on the safe side, and I don't like the witness to miss his flight in any event, but -- but unfortunately, we would request to come back in -- at a time when it would be convenient for you. The Victims and Witness Section will communicate to you to find out what time will suit you. So we have to adjourn your evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is your decision. Your Honour, given my past experience in being a witness at this Tribunal, I'm somewhat surprised. I think I -- the accused has had a great deal of time to question me. He believes that I'm a very important witness. I wouldn't make that claim for myself. I would also like to point out something else to this Tribunal as far as this is concerned. I was first told in November and given a date when I would be a witness to this court. I have been given several other dates since then. On each occasion I've had to change my plans because I had to keep the Tribunal in mind, and on each occasion it was cancelled. November to May is quite a long time to keep being told that you have to change your personal life because you have to be a witness at a Tribunal. I don't know if Your Honours have been a witness at a Tribunal ever in your own lives. It is not a comfortable experience. I feel I have come. We've made time again. Although it has caused problems in my own private life, I have come here this week. I have given the time, and would I agree with the Prosecution that this has been ample. One other point on this, Your Honour, is that in my experience of this court, I have never encountered such muddled questioning and heard so many comments made by the accused or by the representative of the accused, and that, as Your Honours yourselves have pointed out to the accused, has wasted a great time of time. That's his decision. That's not my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I don't want to weigh in long. I would only ask the Court to review the transcript, to reconsider it's -- I don't know that the Court has made an actual decision to recall the witness. Instead to consider that possibility. My recollection is the accused was told how much time he could expect to have, indicated that he was aware of that but might nevertheless make some request for the witness to return, that that would have to be considered in light of the manner in which he used the time he had. The Court encouraged him repeatedly to be more efficient, to ask relevant questions. I think a review of the transcript will reveal that he repeatedly failed to comply with that request, and I think that bears on any request to bring the witness back, particularly in light of the time that the witness has devoted to this process already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The position is never easy. When a witness comes to court to give evidence, he is at large when it comes to cross-examination, but the observations made by this witness mirror the observations that were made from the Bench as to the nature and content of some of the cross-examination, but nevertheless, it remains the position that the defendant must be able to conclude his cross-examination, whether that's done in a manner which is appropriate in terms of absolute efficiency or whether there is a different view as to that efficiency. But the position is this, that normally speaking when a witness comes to court, the time for the witness is predicated by the end of the cross-examination, not predicated by the necessity to catch a particular flight. The reality is in this position that the Court is very happy and wants the witness to catch his flight, and the Court can then consider by looking at the transcripts, and no doubt Dr. Karadzic can reconsider whether it's absolutely necessary to ask Mr. van Lynden to attend again, and if he is asked, he must make his own mind up as to whether he's prepared to come or not prepared to come.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think I would be in contempt of court if I did not return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You may -- that's an arguable proposition, but we're not dealing with that at the moment. Let's -- let's see whether or not it's a necessity, an absolute necessity, and I'm sure Dr. Karadzic has expended a great deal of time, if not all the time that he wanted -- reconsider the position rather than, as it were, to make any definitive statement now and waste more time when you have a flight to catch. I think it's better that all parties consider their decisions and make a rational decision upon a mature reflection of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour. But I would ask that if I do have to return that it be in -- as quickly as possible. Either at the end of next week or the week after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm -- I don't think the Bench can assist with the scheduling in that sense, but no doubt the Prosecution hears what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I don't think I'm allowed to talk to the Prosecution, if my testimony hasn't finished, I would -- I'm trying to send a message to them by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm sure that Dr. Karadzic would not object, nor would the Bench object if you negotiated as to the timings of a return rather than anything substantive in respect of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would ask the victim and witness section to coordinate with the Prosecution as well as the Defence to set a date for Mr. van Lynden to come over again. I do appreciate, Mr. van Lynden, for your kindness to come over yet again to give your testimony and further to agree to come back again. So please do bear in mind in this case your evidence was admitted via written statement, which took several hours to give in it direct. So although your evidence in this case took less than two hours, the accused needs some more time. Thank you very much. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for 15 minutes, and then we'll start -- we'll hear other evidence. Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that there are some administrative matters to be raised. Who is going first? Mr. Nicholls or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just came in to object, Your Honour, if they offered the pages of the Rose book, which I thought we had not yet dealt with and that were shown to Mr. van Lynden just before he departed. I don't believe that they tendered that document and were about to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But e-court says part of that book has been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, but my understanding was that these pages had not been. If it's already, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. Part of the book, I don't know to whom, but which was put to some witness, must have been admitted. That's why we have the exhibit number. Do we know the page number which was -- 174. And I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 18 and 69, 70, if I might be allowed to add. And I'd like to remind you that the witness confirmed that after Markale in February 1994 he was in Sarajevo. So he co-operated with General Rose -- or, rather, could co-operate and could take information from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it is your position to object to admitting those, page 18 and 69 to 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, under the guidelines which we've issued and the general principles. The conversation about the greeting, for lack of a better word, that General Rose described at page 18, the witness said he knew nothing about it, and that nothing like that had happened in his experience. General Rose's comments contained in the book on journalists. The witness again said, That's nothing to do with me, and I can't comment on it. The time-frame wasn't given, and this should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree. I don't recall in what context page 147 of that book was admitted. 174. But in this case --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The witness didn't confirm the content of it, and then could not comment on it, and for the practical purpose to check the credibility of the witness, the crux of the book -- of the pages, those pages, were put to the witness. I don't feel the need to admit those parts. Following our procedure, by principle we do not admit General Rose's book. What is your next agenda, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with respect to the previous question, although you've made a ruling, what I want to say is that Mr. van Lynden confirmed that he did take information and was informed about events at the -- from the United Nations. It's impossible that General Rose would have kept quiet about something that was his generally known position. So that shows a discrepancy there. And the second thing was this: The Defence has nothing against having Mr. van Lynden appear already on Tuesday or when we finish with Mr. Doyle. That was his wish, and perhaps it would be best for everybody concerned, because his testimony will be fresh in our minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it in the hands of the parties. So the parties should communicate through VWS and what date would be most convenient. Is that it? Yes. Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I really would like to urge you to consider whether it is absolutely necessary. I think Mr. van Lynden set out his general position, I think fairly clearly, to all of us in that there were things that he adopted and things that he didn't adopt. And if you are intending to put statements to him in extensio, you're likely to receive the same sort of answers, and a lot of the statements you may, on reflection, feel are better produced through another witness who can speak to the authenticity of the statement and the contents of the statement, rather than simply commenting upon a partial observation or a subjective observation of one or two sentences. You may find that that's actually a much better way to adduce the evidence before the Court, and upon mature reflection that it isn't actually necessary to deal through Mr. van Lynden with that matter. I'm not making any definitive judgements. I couldn't on my own. But it seems to me that that is a valuable exercise which you might want to undertake before requesting Mr. van Lynden's re-attendance at the court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will consider that proposal of yours with my associates and advisors, but we first of all asked for 12 hours for Mr. van Lynden and then 8 hours later on. Now, if he's not coming in next week, we would need next week as a break, and I think that break was promised us when the start of the trial and the proceedings were scheduled, and I think that is to be found in the transcript. I don't know the number of the page transcript number off hand. So we will -- we had to go ahead sooner than we had planned with less time for preparation, especially when we have this very important witness coming in next. So I'll be able to give you a definitive answer when I consult -- having consulted my associates. Now, if Mr. van Lynden is not coming in next week, then if we complete Mr. Doyle's testimony early, the Defence would request that we don't work next week, that the next witness does not come in next week, but that we have a break. Or perhaps just the examination-in-chief and to defer the cross-examination to the week after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will consider when the parties come up with an agreement or suggestion. Let's bring in the next witness. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Before we bring in the next witness, I would like to raise one administrative matter, but we have to do this in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. We will bring in the witness. There will be a slight correction of exhibit number from the Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The two exhibits that were admitted today with the previous witness which were numbered previously as Exhibit D213 and D214 should in fact be Exhibit D211 and D212 respectively. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Doyle. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Microphone. If you could repeat, because it was not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Repeat it? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: My full name is Colm Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you are a retired colonel in the Irish army?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You testified here at the Tribunal already twice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in particular, you testified in the case of the Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic on the 26th and the 27th of August, 2003?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Colonel, have you had an opportunity to review the transcript of your testimony in the Milosevic case when you came here?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in doing so, did you identify three facts that you want to clarify or correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. There were three points which -- which I thought needed correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And in relation to the transcript page 25312 in the Milosevic testimony, were you -- where you discussed with Mr. Milosevic a parliamentary debate on a referendum on independence, did you wish to clarify a date given there by Mr. Milosevic and he spoke about 24th October?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. The 24th of October was a different occasion, and I was referring to the parliamentary debate which took place in -- at a later date than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And which date?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I think that date was in January in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on page 25377, Mr. Milosevic quoted General MacKenzie in relation to the duration of the blockade of the Marsal Tito Barracks to which you responded that that's an impossibility. Mr. MacKenzie was speaking of months, and you said -- and you were referring to your visit there and providing your understanding that the barracks were surrounded for approximately two days. What is the clarification that you wanted to give?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The clarification is that when I was talking about the barracks that was blocked for two days, it wasn't in fact the Marsal Tito Barracks, but it was the headquarters of the federal army based in Sarajevo, which I think was in Bistrik. That's the barracks that I was referring to and not the Marshall Tito.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally on page 2538 there is the date 12 June given as the date on which the European Community Monitoring Mission and you were withdrawn from Sarajevo. Do you wish to correct that date?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. The date in question in fact was the 12th of May, 1992, and not the 12th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the exception of these clarification, can you affirm that the transcript of your testimony in the Milosevic case accurately reflects the evidence you provided to the Court at that time?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Colonel, would you provide that same information to the Court if examined again on the same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this testimony, 65 ter number 90012, for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in sort it's a transcript of his testimony in the case of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and it's now 65 ter number 90012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle's evidence at the time was given pursuant to Rule 92 ter, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Doyle actually gave a quite extensive additional testimony, and we want to tender the -- this testimony. The statement that was the basis for the 92 ter in the Milosevic case is -- was exhibited in the Milosevic case, and it is now our Exhibit Number 10879. We -- I -- we did not produce an amalgamated statement because the evidence in the testimony and the -- the statement are basically the same. The reason why we also, however, want this to be exhibited is that during the testimony in the Milosevic case, the paragraphs in that statement are constantly referred to, in particular by Mr. Milosevic. So therefore at the end I will ask the Judges to also exhibit this statement just as a reference document. It's not that there is something in there which would be different from the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any objection to its admission?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If I get enough time to challenge everything, then it's all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would expect in the future you would produce in such case an amalgamated statement. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I don't want to take time right now, but perhaps that matter can be discussed. I mean, we've taken quite a close look at that, trying to meet both the letter and the spirit of the Court's guidance with respect to that, but this seems to us, upon careful reflection, a matter that does not advance the -- the interests underlying the amalgamated statements. It produces -- it, in fact, is potentially confusion -- confusing and results in, what we would consider, perhaps unnecessary work. In any event, perhaps we can -- we can find a better opportunity to address the pros and cons of the amalgamated statement in this kind of context, and I would just ask that we have that opportunity. But not now. I know we're trying to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, with your permission, I would now read a summary of Colonel Doyle's evidence as admitted. From October 1991 to March 1992, Colonel Doyle served as a member of the European Community Monitoring Mission, the ECMM, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, initially stationed in Banja Luka, and from the 24th of November, 1991, in Sarajevo where he perform duties as the head of the ECMM mission in Sarajevo. During this time, Colonel Doyle met with leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina both on the local level as well as on the republican level, including the accused. He recalls that local Serb -- Serb leaders very often referred back to historical events and atrocities of the Second World War and expressed fears of their repetition. Muslim representatives informed the witness that they were intimidated and afraid to go out at night. Bosnian Serb reservists would return from service and retain their weapons and cause incidents which increased the tension between Serbs and non-Serbs. Colonel Doyle was aware that following the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia, tension grew in areas where the JNA forces were increasing their presence. He observed the transformation of the JNA into a Serbian Army, and the JNA's close relationship with the Bosnian Serbs. From meetings with the accused, Colonel Doyle observed that he was the undisputed head of the Serbian Democratic Party. The Bosnian Presidency members Plavsic and Koljevic and other Bosnian Serb leaders would defer to his decisions. During a meeting with the accused immediately before the referendum on Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence, the accused predicted that there would be a conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would the state internationally be recognised without first reaching an agreement with the Bosnian Serbs. On 2nd March 1992, the day after the results of the referendum were announced, shooting commenced in Sarajevo and barricades were erected by Serbs. Upon approaching one of these barricades, Colonel Doyle was informed by the person in charge that the barricade would only be dismantled upon Karadzic's specific direction. From April 1992 to August 1992, Colonel Doyle functioned as personal representative of Lord Carrington, the chairman of the international peace conference on the former Yugoslavia. In this capacity, he continued to participate in high-level meetings with all sides, including the accused, and to monitor political and military developments. On 10th of April, 1992, Martin Bell of the BBC informed Colonel Doyle that 25.000 refugees were on the move from Zvornik, and Colonel Doyle conveyed this information to the accused. On another occasion, after reports of ethnic cleansing had been received by the ECMM, an ECMM team was dispatched to Foca but was prevented from entering by the JNA forces. Colonel Doyle raised this matter with Mr. Koljevic. Also in April 1992, Colonel Doyle was engaged in cease-fire negotiations. During these negotiations, Bosnian Serb officials sought to divide the assets belonging to the Sarajevo Television. On 18 April 1992, Sarajevo Television received a call from somebody in Pale warning them to get off the air, otherwise they would be destroyed. Colonel Doyle sought and received Karadzic's assurances that this would not happen. About 20 minutes later, Sarajevo Television was shelled by Serb forces, resulting in the death of two civilians. That same evening, the accused acknowledged that the attack had been committed by Serbs but that it was not authorised and that he would investigate the attack. Colonel Doyle observed and was aware of the constant shelling of the city of Sarajevo by Serb forces. He also received reports about sniping activities. The continued shelling of the city meant that on 11 of May, 1992, ECMM monitors and other internationals had to leave, and Colonel Doyle left on the 12th of May. On 3rd July 1992, when Colonel Doyle returned to Sarajevo, he noticed a deterioration of the situation. Each day there was heavy artillery bombardment in the city. On 16 August 1992, whilst in Brussels for negotiations, Colonel Doyle confronted the accused with a "Times" newspaper article carrying a photograph on its front cover of Muslim detainees at a camp in Prijedor. Later that day, the accused expressed concerns about the impact of this news to Colonel Doyle. Colonel Doyle raised with him at that occasion the issue of Muslims and Croats being forced to sign over their property to Bosnian Serbs before leaving. The accused conceded that this was unlawful and stated that he would publicly condemn this practice. Your Honour, this concludes the summary, and I would now ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We haven't given the exhibit number to his had 92 ter statement. Shall we do that now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 90012 will be Exhibit P918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, you have described your functions and your testimony as an impartial observer of the events on the ground. What was the European Community Monitoring Mission's mandate?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the basic mandate of the ECMM was contained in the memorandum of understanding that was signed on the 1st of October, 1991. And the main mission of the ECMM was to attempt to contain the situation, to try and ensure that there would be no escalation or no violence, and if there -- if that was not succeeded by the mission to attain, then to verify the situation so that we could give an accurate picture to headquarters in Europe as to what exactly was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I would ask that exhibit 65 ter 11038 be brought up and page 10 of this -- this exhibit. It's the -- the ERN number 0334-0091.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's not the right one. Page 10 of this particular exhibit. Yeah. Yeah. That's the right one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, is that the memorandum that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And moving on to the pages 16 to 18, the next -- at the end of this particular document, please. Yeah. That's actually sufficient. At the end of this memorandum, there is -- is there a detail of the structure of the mission and the personnel involved?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the structure of the mission for -- for the operation that was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Which was the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit 65 ter 11038 for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P919.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From your service with the Irish army, did you have experience in monitoring activities in crisis or conflict areas before you joined the ECMM mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I served on a few occasions as a member of the Irish defence forces in United Nations peacekeeping missions abroad. I served in Cyprus as a captain in 1968. I was with the first Irish unit to see service in Lebanon with the UNIFIL in 1978. And more importantly, between 1984 and 1986, I was a military observer with the United Nations truce sup division organisation. Six months of that I spent in Syria and a year and a half in Lebanon. So I had some experience in dealing with parties to conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the ECMM mission reports that you have drafted, can you tell the Court what were your sources of information.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the organisation of the monitor mission in Sarajevo had approximately 60 personnel drawn from the countries of the European Union and also from four countries that weren't in the union at the time but they were part of OSCE, the organisation for security and co-operation in Europe. I think they were Poland, Sweden, the Czech Republic or Czechoslovakia at the time, and Canada. So these were mainly military officers who had experience of service abroad and also members of ministries of defence from member states and members of the EU Commission. I had divided these into various teams. So we deployed teams in areas of Bosnia that covered predominantly Serb areas, Croat areas, and Muslim areas, places like Bihac, Tuzla, Banja Luka, Sarajevo, and Mostar, and they would go out into the communities. They would have meetings with the various local political leaders, the religious communities, civilian communities, and even the JNA forces. And they would compile a report which would be submitted back to my office. We would then look at it, analyse it, and we would then make out a consolidated report which we would send to the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. From your contacts with the various leaderships you had yourself of the parties involved, did you get the impression that the parties accepted you as impartial?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I had no reason at all to believe that we were not accepted by all sides. They certainly gave us their co-operation. At meetings we -- we asked. There was never any occasion when we were refused, so we assumed that we were an acceptable, neutral group of people trying to do the job that we were mandated to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned in your previous testimony as well in the reports that were filed at that time that you received information from representatives of the Bosnian government of the build-up by JNA troops in the course of the withdrawal from Croatia and the influx of weapons from the JNA, and that this was perceived as threats and intimidation by the non-Serbs. Did you or the ECMM observers make observations to this effect in the course of your monitoring?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, there were certain trends which came through the reports which were received from all of the areas which were relatively common. And one of those certainly was that it would appear that a lot of the Bosnian Serbs had access to weapons that Muslim and Croats didn't have. So when we tried to examine the background to this, we discovered that first of all the -- when the -- when the JNA called up for mobilisation, the president of Bosnia, Alija Izetbegovic, already indicated that they were declaring a neutrality, and therefore there was no need for people to obey the call-up. But this was done mainly by Bosnian Serbs. In addition to that, when they were issued with weapons, they were allowed to keep the weapons when they finished their few weeks of training. So combined with that and also the fact that when the JNA were withdrawn from Croatia, those members of the JNA who were natives of Bosnia were allowed to stay in Bosnia. And while most of those were actually Bosnian Serbs, they then, practically overnight, became the Bosnian Serb Army, because when the JNA left Croatia and come into Bosnia and then were attempting to leave Bosnia, they handed over quite a considerable amount of tanks, artillery, and most military equipment. So almost overnight the Bosnian Serbs were -- were able to declare themselves that they had an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would -- I would ask that exhibit 65 ter 11098 be brought up on the screen, please. And as this is being done, it is a report of 13 March 1992 on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's a one-page report. Colonel, is this one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just to help us with -- because we see it in many documents, RC Sarajevo stands for what?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The the regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And DHOM?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: DHOM stands for the Deputy Head of Mission, who would have been based in Zagreb at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at letter (b) -- a bit further down, please. Letter (b), there is a reference. In point (b) you speak of an abundant supply of weapons in the Serbian communities. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. That was our -- that was our assessment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender Exhibit 11098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P920.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now ask that Exhibit 65 ter 00039 be brought up onto the screen. And as this is being done, it is the transcript from the 24th session of the RS Assembly, dated 8 January 1993. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, did you -- did you have an opportunity to review this document when you came to The Hague this time, at least in parts?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I had an opportunity of scanning it quickly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 53 in the B/C/S and page 77 in English. And can we -- can we zoom -- no. Okay. If you look at the -- the third paragraph, now starting with, "Now we go back to this."

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You see that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just -- so to say it's Mr. Vojo Kupresanin speaking. This can be seen from the two pages previous. And he is saying: "We had aviation, howitzers, tanks, cannons. But what did the Muslims have? Some guns, some machine-gun that they had bought from the Serbs, and homemade guns. We could have gunned through Bosnia as through cheese, but have not done it." These remarks on the weapons on either side, is this consistent with your own information that you had during the time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is a fair reflection of what we had thought. Of course we weren't naive enough to think that the Croats and the Muslims didn't have weapons. They would have had some weapons, but certainly there was no comparison between the amount that Muslims and Croats would have had and those of the Serbs. They seemed to have them at their disposal in whatever quantities they wished.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have an objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a leading question, so let it be, but may it not happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have to say this is not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She put the text of the transcript of your -- of the Republika Srpska session, and you ask -- she asked whether it's consistent with his impression. No leading question. Let's move on.

It relates to humanitarian matters, lifelong suffering of the Serb people is described, and representation of the various municipality leaders on these issues. So I thought it falls into the -- into the guidelines that we have gotten so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you are going to use this document with upcoming witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I would actually think that Dr. Karadzic would do the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any additional comment, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect to this particular category of documents, the Assembly sessions, I believe the Chamber has already made a determination about their admissibility in their entirety and has done so on previously occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No objections. I'm going to use the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now ask that Exhibit 65 ter 11036 be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel is this one of the weekly reports that you prepared in handwriting at the time you were stationed in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 3 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you read -- can you read paragraph 7 to us, the first paragraph on that page?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: "The presence of so many reservists who are undisciplined and badly behaved is very worrying to Croats and Muslims. The Serbs support the call-up and display a stubborn attitude in this regard."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What you have here mentioned, is this a unique occurrence, or is it something that you observed in other regions as well?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: This is one of the factors that seemed to be current to all of the teams that we had deployed, that there were reservists who were mostly Serbs, because they were armed, they were undisciplined. And at one stage I made an approach to the JNA commander in Banja Luka asking him if he would take action against those who seemed completely undisciplined and not under anybody's control. Now he assured me that this would happen and when he was subsequently replaced by another general, the situation in Banja Luka seemed to be eased somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now the next -- Your Honours, I would like to tender this exhibit. I almost forgot it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P922, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now like to ask Exhibit 11037 be shown. It's a report of the 30th of October, 1991. Is this your report related to a visit to the Manjaca detention facility?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During your term of office, did you get information on other detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: We had heard a lot of reports, rumours, suspicions, that there were other camps that were holding detainees. But as far as I know, we did not get any access to any of these camps because at that time movement was becoming increasingly difficult for the monitor mission. But the camp that I went to in Manjaca was done with the sanction of the JNA forces in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Unless it is objected to, it will be admitted into evidence as ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P923, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, you described the set-up of barricades beginning of March 1992 and the negotiations involved later on to get them removed. I would --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this context I would like to ask that Exhibit 11040 be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a special report on Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 1st and 2nd of March, 1992. Is this your report on the events?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can we please have page 2 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it refers -- in the first paragraph it refers to a group approaching a barricade and the negotiation that followed. Were you in this group, and is that mentioned here in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I was the -- I was organising the group to cross the bridge to try and effect the lifting of the blockade in question, and I was accompanied by the minister of information, Mr. Ostojic. And as it says in the report, the abbreviation there HRC stands for head of regional centre. That was my -- that was me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall the conversation and what was said was needed for dismantling?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asked if -- because the city had been blockaded at this stage, I was asked if I could use my -- my influence or my appointment to try and effect the lifting of the barricades. So I approached one of them and having discussed the matter with the person I spoke with, I asked under what conditions would they be willing to lift the barricade, and he specifically mentioned that the only way -- the only condition under which he would lift the barricade was that if it got the express direction from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P924.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony and reports that the Bosnian government were opposed to the presence of the JNA. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the first time this came to my attention was just after I had assumed the -- the appointment of head of the regional centre, and I was in Sarajevo. It was towards the end of November, and I was requested to meet with the prime minister, who was a Croat, Mr. Pelivan. And I had asked him specifically why there seemed not to be any dealings with the federal army, the JNA. And he replied that as far as he was concerned, and I assume the government was concerned, they looked upon the JNA as an "army of occupation" is the phrase he actually used to me. I suggested that as the JNA were a very potent force based in Bosnia, that it would be better if they opened up some sort of negotiations with them. The issue of the JNA on that occasion was brought up specifically by the prime minister, because he referred to a consignment of rockets that were seized crossing the border if Montenegro into Bosnia. There was no manifest for these. They were contained on four trucks. That didn't -- that they were covered. They weren't military trucks. So they were confiscated by the police, the Bosnian government police. And when they searched, they found that they were full of rockets. So they brought this attention -- they brought this information to the attention, I understand, of the government or the Interior Ministry. And the JNA said that if the government didn't release these rockets to their care, they would take them by force. So my understanding was that the weapons were actually handed over to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 09446 be brought up on onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as we are waiting for it, it is a combat -- an operation report of the 2nd Military District Command, dated 10th of April, 1992. It's both in English and in -- yes. Colonel, did you have the opportunity to review this document when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you have contacts with the 2nd Military District Command?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where was it situated?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the -- it was based in Sarajevo. It was headed by the senior military commander General Kukanjac. And the direct corps based in Sarajevo, I think, was the 4th corps, and that was commanded by General Djudjarevic [phoen]. I had taken it upon myself. I felt it was important for the monitor mission that we had good contacts with the federal army, and therefore I took it upon myself to visit all the major military garrisons throughout the republic. So I went to the garrisons -- the garrisons in -- in Bihac, Banja Luka, Sarajevo itself, and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 3 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English. Yes. And if we zoom in on 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Under point 3 it states in the letter -- rather, in the middle of page -- of paragraph 3 it says: "The president of Bosnia-Herzegovina claims that the JNA is the only force capable of acting to save the Muslim population in Zvornik sector but is unwilling to do so, which will only compound further the hostile stance of the Muslim population towards the JNA." Can you describe what was expected from the JNA and how they indeed acted in Zvornik to your information?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I got some reports from -- from members of the ECMM, but even though I got some reports, they weren't able to verify to me that they were able to in fact get to Zvornik. So what I take from this is that the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina must have been aware that because the JNA were a military force, in times of conflict they would have been the only force that would have been able to protect the Muslims. We had reason to believe that the JNA were used in the area of Zvornik to surround the location and not to allow anybody in or out, but I didn't have first-hand knowledge or evidence of that. So I think that is probably what the president might have been referring to on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P925.
