utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have actually foreseen that, and that's why I am in fact doing this. And I will not address the intercepts because I know the position of this Trial Chamber, except for the one, and that is a very particular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I'm aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break for 15 minutes, and we will end up at 1.30 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, you testified that you spoke about information on ethnic cleansing in Foca with Mr. Koljevic in April 1992. The term "ethnic cleansing," what did you understand it to entail?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, my interpretation of the term "ethnic cleansing" was to be rid of or to expel or to -- basically to -- to expel by force a population from a given area and also to attempt to get rid of all evidence that they would have been in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Evidence of what?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Of personnel. In other words, to expel people by force and to expel all aspects of that race. For example, mosques or institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to ask to have Exhibit 65 ter 11591 on the screen. And as it is being brought up, it is a report of the UN security -- Secretary-General to the Security Council, dated the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have the opportunity to review this document when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we go a bit further down so that we can see paragraph 2. In the very last line you are mentioned as having met Mr. Goulding. Did you brief him, or what were your contacts?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Mr. Goulding had come to Bosnia, and he wanted to meet with the various -- I understand the party leaders and the institutions of government, and I'd been invited to -- to meet with him. At the time, I had been invited to meet him with the force commander General Satish Nambiar, and we had a fairly quick discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 2 of this -- this report on the screen. And I would like to have paragraph 3. Can we zoom in on paragraph 3. Paragraph 3 refers to the situation in Sarajevo, and it says here starting in the third line: "The city -- the city suffers heavy shelling and sniper fire nightly and intermittent shelling at other times, often on a random basis by Serb irregulars in the surrounding hills who use mortars and light artillery allegedly made available to them by the JNA." Colonel, is this consistent with the information you got at that time, that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you yourself experience shelling?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: It was towards the -- it was -- basically it was in April, and I was located for a while in the PTT building. And during certain negotiations I was carrying out, artillery shells were fired, and they landed just outside the PTT building. So there was a certain amount of damage to the building itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the last sentence of that same paragraph there is a reference to the growing shortage of food and other essential supplies owing to the blockade imposed on the city by the Serb forces. Is this consistent with your own observations?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, because there was a certain amount of conflict going on in the city, there were shortages of food, and that even extended to the location that I was in, which was the Serb area Ilidza. We even had shortages there. So it was something that the population on all sides of the city of Sarajevo, those that were there at the time were beginning to suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could we now go to -- further down to paragraph 5, and -- yeah. And I read to you. Here it says: "All international observers agree that what is happening is a concerted effort by the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the acquiesce of, and at least some support from the JNA to create ethnically-pure regions in the context of negotiations on the cantonisation of the republic in the EC Conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina chaired by -- by Ambassador Cutileiro. And the techniques used are the seizure of territory by military force and --" Can we move to the next page. "-- and intimidation of the non-Serb population." And it says here that all observers agree. Did you agree? Was that your assessment?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be much what we would have thought, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of Exhibit 11591.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P937.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During your contacts with the Bosnian Serbs' representatives both on the local and also on the federal republic level, did any of them speak to you about living with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. This particular comment was brought up by an official of the Bosnian Serbs when I went to Pale on the 1st of May, 1992. I don't know in what capacity she was, but certainly she was one of the Bosnian Serb officials I met up there. And she said, Mr. Doyle, you know, I'm quite happy to live with others, but I want a fence built round my house. I will only feel safe if I'm inside my house and I have protection outside. And that was the feeling we got at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 06608 be brought up on the screen. And as it is being done, it is a short-hand transcript of the SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina Deputies Club session of 28 February 1992. Did you have an opportunity to review this document in parts while you were in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have page 33 in English, and 48 in the B/C/S on the screen. And we will see -- we will see that Dr. Karadzic is speaking. That's not seen on that page, but two -- is seen two pages before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic -- I think it's not -- it's -- yes. And page 52 in the B/C/S, and 36 in the English now. And in the -- in the upper part it starts with "Imagine the stupidity." It's the fourth, the fourth paragraph. It says in the fourth paragraph: "Imagine the stupidity of it: The conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is basically a conflict among peoples, just as it was in the case between India and Pakistan, and that's nothing new. It resulted in a huge resettlement of the people. "Muslims cannot live with others. We must be clear on that. They couldn't live with the Hindu who are as peaceful as sheep. That's the Indian religion. They are a peaceful people, and yet they couldn't live with them. They could not live with the Greek on Cyprus. They couldn't live in the Lebanon with Arabs of the same blood, same language, but of a different faith. "There cannot be -- there can be no discussion here. "Yet they set up the Bosnian Krajina there, and in two years' time you have a problem again, to separate each and every village there, because they will overwhelm you with their birth rate and their tricks. We cannot allow that to happen." Colonel, did you see this view reflected by Serb representatives that you met while you were there?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and we were struck by the fact that the Serbs always seemed to refer mainly to the Muslims, even though there were Croats, but it was always the Muslims that they were worried about. And those sentiments that appear in that report would be -- would be much the same that we gathered ourselves. That was our impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, it's in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, because it's again the same situation, contemporaneous official document, and I'm sure that other witnesses will refer to it, and also, most likely, Dr. Karadzic would like to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you object to its admission?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection. I was just waiting for the interpretation. No, I don't have any objections, except to say that I'm going to have to tender more documents, because this isn't the only place where I address that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P938, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the number. Is it P938? Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I would ask now that Exhibit 65 ter 40174 be played, and it's actually a video footage depicting speeches on the 21st Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 30th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before we play it, did you have an opportunity to see part of this footage and the transcript in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we play now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] This is the 21st session of our Assembly, and the path behind us is so rich that many things occur between two sessions. This is actually the path that gradually brought us to our state, taking us from an artificial state in which we were forcibly -- forcefully held in an artificial creation, this Bosnia and Herzegovina, with our centuries-old foes. It all reminds me of the experiment in which a dog and a cat are held in a box against their will, or a bad marriage maintained by all sorts of forceful means. It transpired that a dog and a cat can remain in a box together only under one condition, namely that they lose their natural characteristics and cease to be a dog and a cat. We will remember that we could not be Serbs and live in such a box."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, when speaking to Bosnian Serbs, did they ever express such views about the Muslim people being their foes, essentially old foes being their enemies?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I think most of the reference that was made by the Bosnian Serbs was the fact that they simply couldn't live with the Muslims. I don't know that I recall any incident where they actually said foes. But certainly there was no doubt in our mind that they were not happy to live with them in a -- the same location. And this would have been borne out, I suppose, by the time I met that lady from the Bosnian Serbs up in Pale. So it was something which they repeatedly referred back to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would request the admission of Exhibit 40174. It's actually quite a big one. My suggestion would be to just admit the speech that Mr. Karadzic does, and that would be the -- the ERN number 0096-8187 to 0096-8192, because the following clips are basically the other people speaking, and that's not a quote from -- from the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't note the starting time, but the ending time says is 1 minute, 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The starting time, I had it somewhere. It starts at zero. Yes, indeed, from the very start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P939, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, in your testimony you describe a conversation with Ms. Plavsic in Pale or on the way to Pale about the entitlement the of Serbs to 70 per cent of the territory. Do you recall when you had this conversation?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. It was when I was on my way up to Pale on May the 1st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And why did you go to Pale together with Ms. Plavsic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I was invited up by the Bosnian Serbs. They had moved most of their personnel from Sarajevo at that stage, and I was conscious that I didn't want to go up there as the head of the monitor mission and somehow be photographed with them so they would say this is a sort of recognition of the entity of the Bosnian Serbs. So I told them that we didn't want any publicity, and this was agreed to. So on the way up, I originally tried to get up there the day before, which was the last day of April, but such were the amount of tanks and artillery pieces and military equipment that was moving up on the main supply route to Pale that we couldn't actually get to Pale itself, and Mrs. Plavsic asked if I would return the following day when we might have a better chance. So I did that the following day, which was, as I say, May the 1st. And in going up there with her, she expressed certain views. She intimated to me that Bosnian Serbs were used to living in wide spaces, and therefore they needed room to move round. She mentioned to me that Muslims were practically people who were business, and therefore would be normally domiciled in a city, and therefore did not need as much territory as the Serbs would need it. And then she said something to me which I will always remember, she said, You know, Mr. Doyle, if it takes the lives of 3 million people to solve this crisis, let's get it done and move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now ask that Exhibit 21082 be put on the screen, 65 ter exhibit. And it is, as we are waiting, it is a transcript of an intercept depicting Mr. Koljevic calling Mr. Mladjo Karisik, from Lisbon. Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you provide the transcript of this intercept to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, earlier on. This transcript was personally given to me by the deputy mayor -- or the deputy prime minister of Bosnia, Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, and I was quite surprised when I saw a transcript which had my name in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And if you -- can we zoom in? It's in -- the latter part is the reference. It's: "Listen, you should take care of that today. We agreed with Doyle to get the observers on the place where our artillery stands. Let that artillery withdraw. We can't start the Conference here without doing this [sic]." As far as this intercept refers to you, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. This was -- this was the same day that I went up to Pale. That was one of the other reasons why we went up there, because there were peace talks being held, I think, in Lisbon. I was asked by Ambassador Cutileiro if I would go to Pale, because according to him the Bosnian Serbs had intimated their willingness to withdraw some of their weapons from the general area. So I took with me my deputy who was Mr. Jeremy Braid, and while I stayed in Pale at the Bosnian Serb headquarters, if you would like, he was taken by the Bosnian Serbs to -- in a car to -- to look, to find out, to ascertain whether or not the artillery was being withdrawn. He had a better idea than I had where the artillery pieces were. But when he returned he told me that there was absolutely no evidence that the artillery was withdrawn, and on the basis of that I recommended that the talks be stopped in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And were they stopped?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I understand that they were, but I -- I can't be sure exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the admittance of this exhibit into evidence, because I think it's a different situation than the other intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This is what a witness received from --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- somebody contemporaneously. Do you have any objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that it would be a good idea if we were to know how come Mahmutcehajic had this conversation, because we were also part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government, a third of the government. We weren't rebels of any kind, but we were part of the government, and the government is mentioned here and some Serbs. So how come Mahmutcehajic has this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's subject for your cross-examination. Yes. We will admit this, but Mr. -- Colonel Doyle, do you hear who intercepted this conversation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P940.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel, in your testimony you spoke about the fact that non-Serb personnel in the Hotel Bosna in Ilidza, where you and also Dr. Karadzic were staying, was forced to leave and that they were expelled. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: This happened around the period, I would think, of March 1992. And it was memorable because there was already conflicts starting in the city, and the dining area where we were had been moved because of the chance of -- of a shooting at the hotel. And I was struck by being -- by the fact that I was invited by the local Serb council, as it were. I'd never met any of them before, which was a surprise to me, and the entire -- almost the entire hotel staff were different to those that I knew for the many months I was there as head of the mission. And when I inquired of -- from this -- this person who intimated that he was now the new leader of the local community he told me that the Muslims were moved, they were put onto a truck, and they were taken into the centre of the city and they were then released. What I remember in particular was I asked him were any -- was there any Muslim member of the staff retained? And he said, "Yes, we kept one because he is a good cook."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Now, you refer in your testimony to a session of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia on the 13th of August, 1992, and you described the situation where you showed Dr. Karadzic a photo of the detainee from a camp in Prijedor, and how you then spoke with him about the pressure of non-Serbs signing over their property before leaving. How did you get aware of this practice of signing over property?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, we had received a considerable amount of information from the monitor mission. That part of the modus operandi, if you were -- if you wish, of the Bosnian Serbs was that they were taking some territory and part of the policy was to ensure that the territory they were taking, that those resident therein actually sign their property away. And this may have been contained in that "Sunday Times" report as part of the article containing that photograph which I gave to Mr. Karadzic. And following on from that, when he saw this, he sent somebody, I think it was a Mr. Kennedy who was advising him, if I would agree to meet with him. So I replied that I wasn't part of the official delegation, but that if we -- if we met in the lobby, I would -- I would certainly speak with him. So when we did that, I brought this question of signing away their property, and he admitted to me that it was wrong and that it was illegal. And I suggested that maybe as a gesture he might send a letter to the "Times" indicating that -- or sending a message out there that he agreed that it was illegal and this should not be done. So he intimated to me that he certainly would do something about it. I don't know whether that was done or not. I -- I have no -- I have no evidence one way or the other as to where -- whether that was done by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 01136 be brought up on the screen. And as we are waiting, it is a report on a meeting in the context of the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You attended this conference and this meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And let me -- let's just go to page 2. Page 2 in paragraph 5, just at the end is -- just the last two sentences, it is says here: "Dr. Karadzic had said that he had issued instructions to stop these forces from harassing those Muslims and Croats who were willing to leave Serbian areas from signing papers to that effect. He confirmed that such papers would have not have validity in the light of a final settlement." This document, did you receive it, this document about the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I received a copy of that at the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to request admittance of this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P941.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You described throughout your testimony meeting Dr. Karadzic and other Serb representatives, and you stated that he was the undisputed leader and that the other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership referred to him. Did you actually observe him interacting with these other leaders?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I remember in -- I think it was January or February of 1992. Because Mr. Karadzic was the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, I asked for a meeting with him. And this was arranged through the Serb members of the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic and Nikolai Koljevic. And I met him there and spoke with him because I wanted to meet the -- all the political leaders of the various parties. And since then when I was either head of the mission or whether I was -- or Lord Carrington's personal representative, at any session that we had with Bosnian Serbs Dr. Karadzic was always there. And he could have been there with -- with Nikola Koljevic, and maybe just the two of them, or with Mr. Krajisnik. But Dr. Karadzic was always there himself. And they always deferred to him. He spoke English. And in my mind, you know, when you attend a lot of these meetings, you get a sense of who is the person that is the leader. And in my view he was the undisputed leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your testimony, you also described the shelling of the TV station in Sarajevo and the contacts that you had with the accused to this effect. Why did you turn to Dr. Karadzic to prevent the attack on the TV?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I received a phone call in the afternoon from the television station to say that they had received a phone call from Pale, from the Bosnian Serbs to say that if they didn't get off the air within 30 minutes, that the television station would be attacked with -- with weapons. So at that time, Mr. Karadzic had the Bosnian Serb Crisis Committee stationed in the Hotel Bosna, in Ilidza. So I decided to make an approach to him. And I spoke to one of his officials and said that it was very important that he get this message to Mr. Karadzic. So he did, and the same -- I assume that he did, because within about 20 minutes he -- he came back to me and what he said was that -- that he spoke to Mr. Karadzic, and I should not worry because this attack would not take place. The attack did take place. The television station was -- I think it was mortar bombed, and my understanding is that there was either two or three people killed. When I got information of this, I immediately contacted that official. I asked him to tell Mr. Karadzic that the attack took place, that there were casualties, and that I was going to hold him personally responsible. Sometime later that evening Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic came to see me, and they were quite agitated. Mr. Karadzic acknowledged that the attack had taken place, but he intimated to me that -- that he hadn't ordered it, that he had condemned it, and that I would have to realise that he didn't control all of the military all of the time. And therefore he couldn't -- I suppose he didn't want to accept responsibility for what some people had done. So he did say to me that it wasn't authorised. But I did mention to him that part of the responsibility of leadership is that you take responsibility for what your subordinates do or fail to do. And therefore I was going to condemn this attack on television which I did later on that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you mentioned -- when you spoke about this during the previous testimony and also in documents, you use the term "Serb paramilitaries." What do you mean by using the term "Serb paramilitaries"?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, part of the peacekeeping operations in my experience was that you don't go looking for specific information on military units because then people have an opportunity of saying you're spying or you're an agent. So I was very careful that I try and maintain a neutral stance. So my interpretation of a paramilitary is if a Serb paramilitary or a Muslim was somebody who bore weapons, who was not in the federal army, in other words, all of those outside the JNA, because there were so many different groups, there were the Muslim Eagles or the Green Berets, and therefore it was -- it was common for us to refer to all non-military JNA who were armed or wore some uniforms and some didn't. So we referred to them collectively, simply as paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And my last question is, did Dr. Karadzic have control over these Bosnian Serb paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I always assumed that he did, because as the -- as the conflict escalated, he seemed to be always in the presence of people who were armed who were close to him. Some of those were wearing the uniforms of the JNA on occasions, and sometimes they weren't. So it was my -- I suppose it was my interpretation or my view that, as the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, that he controlled or should have had control over all aspects of -- of the Bosnian Serbs, and that would include armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did he attend cease-fires when you had negotiations? Did Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. He attended -- he attended all of the cease-fires that I was involved in with the exception of a cease-fire that was negotiated shortly after the time in which the president -- we successfully negotiated the release of President Izetbegovic. And at those cease-fire agreements, it was basically -- we were concentrating on attempting to get an agreement for the withdraw of the federal army from -- from Bosnia. We had -- we had invited the Bosnian Serbs, but they didn't come to the PTT building, I believe because they were worried about security and most of them now were based in balances, and that was understandable. But even though we invite them to come, they didn't attend those sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes the examination-in-chief. In relation to the remaining associated exhibits, I would request to admit them, except for the one that you yourself mentioned. We do not ask admittance because it's basically related -- unrelated to this case. And I also will not ask for the admittance of the intercepts, but I would request the admission of Exhibit 11087, and that's the witness declaration as to the voices he recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What you exclude from the associate exhibit is, to be clear, 11069; and two intercepts, 30323 and 30423.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Two intercepts? No. The -- what I had actually said is the intercepts that are listed, they will be introduced through other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are not tendering those two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which two? No, it's actually more than two. It's more than two. It's -- the intercepts -- sorry, Your Honour. The intercepts, I gave range -- a range. The intercepts starting 30323, down to 0 -- 31614. So it's basically altogether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- quite a number of intercepts. They will be introduced otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there are no intercepts, I have no objections in relation to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be all admitted and assigned exhibit number, the numbers of which will be circulated in due course by the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We have about 15 minutes. So will you start your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are going to go on working today, then, yes, I shall certainly start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Once again, I wish to thank you for your kindness to meet up with the Defence and help us shed more light on certain matters. Now I would like us to recall together what it was that we possibly agreed upon during that meeting. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we agreed that the Muslims had rejected calls for mobilisation. It's not that they were excluded from the JNA in some other way. Namely, they did not respond to mobilisation, and thereby the Serbs became the only mobilisation base for the JNA at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, we agreed that you did not have any particular knowledge about the situation in Yugoslavia before you came there, that you did not have dealings with Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I'd received a standard operational briefing from our military headquarters on the situation, but -- but no specific details. So I would agree generally with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have agreed -- or, rather, you confirmed something that worried me a bit. After 18 years, one's memory does fade a bit, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I have to admit to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agreed that you did not quite understand the political manoeuvres within Bosnia-Herzegovina at a high level, at policy-making level, as it were. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we agreed and that you confirmed that the Serbs wanted greater access to TV Sarajevo -- or, rather, more of a presence at TV Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. There was a different interpretation as to the discussions we had on what the people that I represented meant by having greater access and what I believe the Bosnian Serbs wanted. The inference on the arrangements we had was that it was fair that the Bosnian Serbs should have more access time to the Television Sarajevo, whereas the interpretation of what the Bosnian Serbs thought they wanted or what they thought they were entitled to was to actually divide the assets of the television station. So they'd get so many studios. They'd get so many percentage of the buildings, and that they would get things like the -- the vehicles, et cetera. This was not what was in mind when we held those peace talks, and therefore, we held a meeting at the television station about two days after the cease-fire was signed, and when I realised that the Bosnian Serbs wanted physical occupation on a permanent basis of the television station, I decided that this was not what was intended and therefore we made no progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that I presented that to you as the establishment of three national channels for the three national groups within a joint television we cannot be treated equally unless we have our TV channel, in our own language, involving our own culture, and meeting our own needs, and that therefore we needed our own studio?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I know that that's what you intended when we spoke last Monday, and I can understand that, but when the negotiations were going on on the ground in Bosnia, that was never the argument, in my view, at that time. Had that been the case, those of us who were involved in negotiations would have made a decision, I think, one way or the other. So my understanding is that at those negotiations it was that the Bosnian Serbs would get more access to television time, which would obviously have included giving over the airwaves their views of certain matters but not the physical assets of the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your opinion what was it that the Muslims wanted as far as television was concerned? What was their concept of television? What was it that that they wanted?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I have no idea what the Muslims wanted because they were happy with the way things were. And at no stage do I recall the Muslims actually raising the issue of television coverage as a matter of concern. The only point I can say that they did mention was that the relay stations which gave coverage to a wider audience were, according to them, distorted physically so that the -- that these things would -- that the range would point towards Belgrade rather than the rest of Bosnia. But apart from that, I don't recall any incident where they were specific as to what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, now we're going to see what they wanted, although you said that they were happy with what they had. Are you aware of the fact that to this day Croats are asking for their own channel? Serbs do have their own television, but to this day the Croats have been asking for a channel of their own because they haven't got one.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of this, because my -- my up-to-date information on the day-to-day life of Bosnia is not something which I have much attention to. So I'm unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but I believe that you will take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have D148. 1D48 in e-court. I hope that we have a translation. No, this is not the document. No, no. That's not the document. This seems to be 148, but I need 1D48. There should be a translation. Could we have the English version as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, may I draw your attention to this letter. It is a letter sent to the SDA personnel committee on the 23rd of March -- or the 20th of March. That is to say -- no, no, no. No. Actually, two weeks before recognition. This is what it says here the Party of Democratic Action, the chairman of the SDA City Board, Harun Imamovic, is asking for the following: "Dear sir: At the 75th session of the Sarajevo SDA City Board held on the 17th of March, 1992, a conclusion was made to address you with a suggestion that you take timely steps to resolve the personnel-related problems at Sarajevo RTV. "The relevance and importance of this institution for all segments of social and political life goes without saying. "The Sarajevo SDA City Board believes that every division of Sarajevo TV into ethnic channels is out of the question, as it would not suit the interests of the Muslim people. "In addition, we would like to say that in order to protect our ethnic interests, it is imperative that the general manager of the RTV be a Muslim, as well as the editor-in-chief of the RTV. "We deem this to be the minimum beneath which no talks should be held." First question: Does the SDA think, based on what is said here, what I believe as well, it is a division of channels that is being referred to, not a division of property, assets?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I would accept that's what the content of the letter would indicate. I notice the letter isn't signed, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the original on the left is signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second question: Do you agree that the interest of the Muslim people is singled out here and placed above the interests of the Serb and Croat peoples? I take you to the following sentence: "The city board of the SDA believes that every division of Sarajevo TV into ethnic channels is out of the question." And let us see why. "And it would not suit the interests of the Muslim people." Do you agree that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in addition to the Muslim people, there were Serbs and Croats who accounted for the Christian majority of that country?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Third question: Do you see that the minimum they are asking for in this joint TV, in the joint country, and how they envisage a life together and democracy, you see that they ask that the director and the editor-in-chief of the RTV have to be Muslims. Does that explain the position that Mrs. Plavsic expressed, that it is hard to live in that kind of situation? Is this a fair claim, to ask for the TV to belong to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, I would agree that the content of the letter would indicate that the Muslim population were looking for an unreasonable demand. I don't think I would equivocate this with the phrase that Mrs. Plavsic, however, spoke with me about it, because I don't think they are related.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do agree that it is hard for the Christian majority, even if it were a minority, to imagine this kind of TV Sarajevo, namely that this Christian majority cannot be represented properly because that does not suit the interests of the Muslim people; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Yes. I've already indicated that, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to leave that material that is based on our interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can this be admitted, this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'd like to continue? One more question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I put it to you, Mr. Doyle, that it was not our position that we could not live with the Muslims, rather, it was the that we could not live under the Muslims. Since you came in 1991, may I remind you that we had proposed to the Muslims that they stay with us in Yugoslavia and that in that case we could have lived with them. Are you aware of that? Also, that this constitutes lack of understanding. It's not a question of not wanting to live with Muslims but not wanting to live understand Muslims.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: Well, the reference I made to the comment passed when I went up to Pale by that Bosnian Serb official certainly did not make any reference to living with or living under. So I can only -- I can only refer back to what she said. And to the extracts that were taken that have been shown here from the -- from -- from your own official Bosnian Serb documents, I'm not too sure that I know of any document which actually states that you would live underneath the Muslims, because I'm not too sure what that really means. There are three sides in Bosnia. There was the Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs, and Bosnian Croats, and I'm not too sure why we should say that the Bosnian Serbs should live under the Bosnian Muslims. I don't quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the previous document telling enough in terms of what our equality of rights would be in that state in we have the document here on our screens?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE
utterances.text: The document on the screen, to my interpretation, deals specifically with an issue of television. It doesn't -- it doesn't encompass all of life in Bosnia. It refers specifically to the rights or the demands for different channels on television, which I can understand. But that doesn't mean in my view that that has to transfer itself to all aspects of life in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that question, we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- we will adjourn for today. We will resume on Wednesday next week at 9.00. Please have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
